slides.text:
In Go, the text `"42"` and the number `42` are different things, and Go never turns one into the other for you. The `strconv` package does it.

In this module you convert text to ints, floats and bools and back, in other bases, and deal with text that is not a number.

Reading text can fail: `"abc"` is not a number. So the functions that read text return two values: the result and an **error**. The error is `nil` when all went well.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.

`Atoi` reads text as an `int`, and `Itoa` writes an `int` as text. Atoi can fail, so it returns an error too. Itoa cannot fail, so it returns only the text.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
Atoi "42"   -> 42, no error
Atoi "abc"  -> 0, an error
Itoa 42     -> "42"

exercises.title: Text to int
exercises.guide: Read a text as an int, and use the number.

chunks.guide: Atoi gives back the number and an error. Print both.

notes.text: Reads a text as an int.
The number, and nil when it worked.

chunks.guide: The result is a real int, so math works on it.

exercises.title: Check the error
exercises.guide: Bad text does not crash the program. It gives an error.

chunks.guide: Convert a text that is not a number. Print the result and the error.
Check the error before using the number. Stop when it failed.

output.text:
0 strconv.Atoi: parsing "abc": invalid syntax
not a number

exercises.title: Check before use
exercises.guide: Read the text as an int, and stop when the conversion failed.

exercises.title: A decimal text
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
n, err := strconv.Atoi("3.5")
fmt.Println(n, err != nil)
exercises.explanation: Atoi reads only whole numbers and never rounds. A decimal text is an error, and the number comes back as 0.

exercises.title: Int to text
exercises.guide: Turn an int into text, and see why string() is not the way.

chunks.guide: Build a text that holds a number.

notes.text: Writes an int as text. It cannot fail.

chunks.guide: `string` on a number gives the character with that code. Itoa gives the digits.

exercises.title: Plus on texts
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
a := strconv.Itoa(7)
b := strconv.Itoa(8)
fmt.Println(a + b)
exercises.explanation: Itoa gives texts, and `+` on texts joins them. The numbers are never added.

slides.text:
The other types follow the same pattern: a `Parse` function reads text and returns an error too, and a `Format` function writes text. The extra arguments say the size in bits, and for ints, the base.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
ParseFloat text, size
ParseBool  text
ParseInt   text, base, size
FormatInt  number, base

exercises.title: Text to float
exercises.guide: Read a text as a float64.

chunks.guide: ParseFloat works like Atoi: the number and an error.

notes.text: Reads a text as a decimal number.
The size in bits: 64 gives a float64.

chunks.guide: It also reads the exponent form. A blank name drops the error, so do it only for text you know is good.

notes.text: The blank name throws the error away.

exercises.title: Float to text
exercises.guide: Write a float as text with a set number of decimals.

chunks.guide: FormatFloat takes the value, a format letter, the decimals and the size.

notes.text: The plain decimal format, like the %f verb.

chunks.guide: With -1 decimals it keeps only the digits needed. With 0 it rounds to a whole number.

notes.text: As many decimals as the value needs.

exercises.title: Read and write a float
exercises.guide: Read the text as a float, then write it back with two decimals.

exercises.title: Text to bool
exercises.guide: Read a bool from text, and write one back.

chunks.guide: ParseBool accepts true, false, 1, 0, t and f, in a few cases.

notes.text: Reads a bool: 1, t, true and True all work.

chunks.text:
ok, err := strconv.ParseBool("true")
    fmt.Println(ok, err)
    yes, _ := strconv.ParseBool("1")
    no, _ := strconv.ParseBool("F")
    fmt.Println(yes, no)

chunks.guide: Other words are an error, and the value is false. FormatBool goes the other way.

notes.text: Writes a bool as true or false.

chunks.text:
maybe, err := strconv.ParseBool("yes")
    fmt.Println(maybe, err)
    fmt.Println(strconv.FormatBool(true))

output.text:
true <nil>
true false
false strconv.ParseBool: parsing "yes": invalid syntax
true

exercises.title: Numbers in a base
exercises.guide: Read and write ints in other bases.

chunks.guide: ParseInt takes the text, the base and the size. Here the text is in base 16.

notes.text: Like Atoi, with a base and a size.
Base 16, and an int64 as the result.

chunks.guide: Base 2 reads binary. Base 0 follows the prefix, so 0x means hex.

notes.text: Base 0 picks the base from the prefix.

chunks.text:
bin, _ := strconv.ParseInt("1011", 2, 64)
    prefixed, _ := strconv.ParseInt("0x1f", 0, 64)
    fmt.Println(bin, prefixed)

chunks.guide: FormatInt writes an int64 in any base.

exercises.title: Too big for 8 bits
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
n, err := strconv.ParseInt("300", 10, 8)
fmt.Println(n, err != nil)
exercises.explanation: An 8 bit int holds up to 127. A bigger value is an error, and the number returned is the largest one that fits.

slides.text:
`Quote` wraps a text in double quotes and escapes what needs it, and `Unquote` undoes it.

Real input is mixed: some pieces convert and some do not. After each conversion you decide what to do with a failure: skip the piece, use a default, or stop.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.

exercises.title: Quote and unquote
exercises.guide: Wrap a text in quotes, and take the quotes off.

chunks.guide: Quote also escapes special characters, such as a tab.

notes.text: Adds the double quotes, like the %q verb.

chunks.guide: Unquote needs a text that has quotes around it. Without them it is an error.

notes.text: The text without quotes, and an error.

chunks.text:
text, err := strconv.Unquote("\"go\"")
    fmt.Println(text, err)
    _, err = strconv.Unquote("go")
    fmt.Println(err)

exercises.title: Quote and back
exercises.guide: Wrap the text in quotes, then take the quotes off again.

exercises.title: Sum a line of numbers
exercises.guide: Add up the numbers of a line and skip the words that are not numbers.

chunks.guide: A line of numbers with one bad word, and a total to fill.
Convert each word. When it fails, move on to the next one.
Only the good words were added.

exercises.title: A default on error
exercises.guide: Write a function that falls back to a default port.

chunks.guide: Return the default when the text is not a number.
A good text, a bad one and an empty one.

exercises.title: What is this function for?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what it is for.
options: Converts a text into an int
Checks that an int is not zero
Checks that a text is a whole number
Prints the error of a conversion
exercises.explanation: The number is thrown away and only the error is used. The function answers whether the text converts.

exercises.title: Spaces around a number
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Atoi fails on spaces, and the number would be 0. TrimSpace removes them first, so the result is 42 plus 1.
